config.title: Course Schedule (Topological Sort)

intro.title: Course Schedule (Topological Sort)
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a program that checks if it's possible to complete all courses given their prerequisites, using the topological sort algorithm. You will learn how to model course dependencies as a graph and detect cycles to determine if a valid schedule exists. The main technologies involved are JavaScript arrays, objects for adjacency lists, and depth-first search (DFS) traversal. This beginner-friendly project will help you understand graph algorithms and their application in scheduling lessons.
intro.usecase: Topological sorting is essential for managing dependencies in real-world systems like package managers (npm, pip), build tools (Make, Webpack), and task schedulers. Developers use it to determine installation orders, compile source files in correct sequence, or schedule interdependent jobs. In UI development, it helps render component trees with proper parent-child relationships or process form validations with field dependencies. Understanding this algorithm helps you design systems that handle complex dependency chains efficiently.

objectives: Construct a graph adjacency list from course prerequisites data
Initialize and maintain indegree arrays to track prerequisite dependencies
Implement a queue-based topological sorting algorithm
Manipulate graph nodes and edges to simulate course enrollment order
Apply topological sort to detect cycles in course prerequisites
Render a valid course schedule when no cycles are present
Configure the algorithm to return an empty array when scheduling is impossible

content.body: Have you ever tried to take courses that depend on each other? Some courses require you to complete others first. Today we'll learn how to check if you can finish all courses without getting stuck in a circular dependency. We'll use a graph algorithm called topological sort.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
1. Explain what topological sort means in course scheduling.
2. Apply the concept of 'visited' nodes to avoid cycles in a graph.
3. Implement a function to check if all courses can be finished given prerequisites.
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Imagine you have 3 courses: A, B, and C. Course B requires A, and Course C requires B. Can you take all three? Think about the order you'd need to follow.
content.title: Try it

content.body: Now suppose Course A also requires C. So A needs C, C needs B, and B needs A. Can you find an order to take them? Try tracing the dependencies.
content.title: Add a twist

content.body: What if you have 4 courses where D requires C, C requires B, B requires A, and that's it? Can you take all four? Notice how you can go from A to D without revisiting any course.
content.title: One more

content.body: You manually traced through course dependencies, checking if you could visit each course without getting stuck in a loop. That's the core challenge in course scheduling.
content.title: What you did

content.body: When there are hundreds of courses with complex prerequisites, manually checking becomes impossible. We need a systematic way to explore the network without going in circles. Can't figure it out? Let's see the approach.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: In graph exploration, we need to track which nodes (courses) we've already visited. This prevents us from revisiting the same node endlessly, especially if there's a cycle. Think of it like leaving a breadcrumb at each course you've checked.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Show visited vs unvisited nodes; paths without going in circles.

content.body: We'll use Depth-First Search (DFS) with three states for each course: unvisited, visiting (currently in the DFS stack), and visited (fully processed). If we encounter a course that's currently 'visiting', we've found a cycle and can't finish all courses.
content.title: The approach

content.body:
1. Build an adjacency list from prerequisites.
2. Initialize a state array for all courses (0 = unvisited, 1 = visiting, 2 = visited).
3. For each course, if unvisited, start DFS.
4. In DFS, mark as visiting, then check prerequisites.
5. If a prerequisite is visiting, cycle detected → return false.
6. If DFS completes without cycles, mark as visited.
7. If all courses visited without cycles, return true.

content.body: Great work! You've implemented topological sort for course scheduling. Key takeaways: 1. Always track 'visited' states to avoid infinite loops in graphs. 2. Use DFS with three states (unvisited, visiting, visited) to detect cycles efficiently. 3. This approach scales to large course networks because each course is processed only once.
content.title: Done
